newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Moslems increasingly at risk in Croat-held Mostar.
newsitem.headline: Moslems increasingly at risk in Croat-held Mostar.

text.p: Fear gripped minority Moslems in Croat-dominated west Mostar on Tuesday after Croats opened fire on Moslem pilgrims trying to visit a cemetery.

NATO-led peacekeeping troops and Western envoys struggled to defuse tensions in the divided Bosnian city a day after Croats shot and stabbed Moslems who had sought to mourn loved ones in Liska cemetery in the Croat-held western quarter.

As international police monitors investigated the violence that killed one Moslem and wounded at least 20, U.N. human rights workers reported an alarming upsurge in expulsions and intimidation of Moslems remaining in west Mostar.

Some Moslems fearful of overnight assault temporarily vacated their flats and slipped into Moslem-controlled east Mostar. When they tried to return home after daybreak, they were blocked by Croat police, Western relief workers said.
Croat militants, tolerated or assisted by Croat police, began evicting more Moslems from flats hours after Monday's daytime incident, U.N. police workers and relief officers said.
International Police Task Force (IPTF) officers, who are unarmed and have no powers of arrest, received telephone calls from Moslems pleading for help.
But IPTF members were ordered to stay in their stations as part of alert measures prompted by violence earlier in the day.
The U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) sought to pin down the number of evictions after receiving unconfirmed reports that at least a dozen families had been expelled.
NATO said earlier that some 26 people were reported evicted overnight, most from a building opposite the main Croat police station in west Mostar.
One Moslem said his 52-year-old mother, Fatima Handac, was ejected from her flat at about 11 p.m. (2200 gmt) by two men wearing masks and carrying pistols.
"I was on the east side when it happened," he said. "They threatened her and kept asking 'Where is your son?'".
He said the Croats dumped his mother in midwinter cold near the former frontline separating Croat and Moslem sectors of Mostar. "They ... told her never to come back," he said.
He and other Moslems went for help at the UNCHR office on Tuesday, queueing up to be interviewed by human rights workers.
Clutching plastic bags with a few meagre belongings, some of the women wept as they recounted their ordeal. The UNHCR said it was struggling to find accommodation for the displaced.
Until Monday, 82 cases of evictions from west Mostar had been recorded since December 1995, when the Dayton peace agreement halted 43 months of nationalist fighting in Bosnia.
Relief workers said Croat police were now also blocking Moslems trying to cross back into west Mostar after day trips to the east in what amounted to de facto evictions.
Hasan Djemal, a Moslem, and his Serb wife Gora said Croat police stole their papers and the keys to their flat when they tried to walk back to the west side on Tuesday morning.

Djemal said he was taken to a police station where two policemen beat his back and head with batons. After 20 minutes at the station, Djemal and his wife were driven to a school which lies on the edge of the Moslem-controlled east side.
The family had already been robbed last autumn and had no relatives in eastern Mostar to rely on, Djemal's wife said.
"I don't see any future. I don't have one. We have no money and no place to sleep here. But we can't go back to west Mostar," she said.
